read.sections.0.text.source: The Banda Islands are small islands in eastern Indonesia. For hundreds of years, they were the only place in the world where nutmeg trees grew. The tree's seed gives nutmeg, and the red skin around the seed gives a spice called mace. Buyers far away paid a lot for both. Traders came from Indonesia, China, India, Persia and Arabia. Later, ships came from Portugal, the Netherlands and England. Bandanese leaders were skilled traders, and they chose whom to sell to. Selling spice also paid for food, because the islands grew very little.
read.sections.0.text.back: The Banda Islands are small islands in eastern Indonesia. For hundreds of years, these islands were the only place in the world where nutmeg trees grew. The tree's seed gives nutmeg, and the red membrane that wraps the seed gives a spice called mace, or nutmeg flower. Buyers in faraway places paid a lot for both. Traders came from Indonesia, China, India, Persia and Arabia. Later, ships came from Portugal, the Netherlands and England. Banda's leaders were skilled traders, and they chose whom they sold to. Selling spice also paid for food, because the islands produced only very little food.
read.sections.0.text.note: "Traders came from Indonesia, …": "Indonesia" kept as in the English (and the diagram), although the islands were not yet called Indonesia; "Nusantara" or "pulau-pulau lain di Nusantara" would read more naturally to Indonesian learners. "Arabia" → "Arab". "The red skin around the seed" → "selaput merah" (the red membrane, the aril).

read.sections.0.simpler.source: The Banda Islands are in Indonesia. For a long time, only Banda had nutmeg trees. Nutmeg is a spice from the seed. Mace is a spice from the red skin on the seed. People far away paid a lot for them. Traders came from many places in Asia, and later from Europe. Banda's leaders were good traders. They chose who to sell to.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: The Banda Islands are in Indonesia. For a long time, only Banda had nutmeg trees. Nutmeg is a spice from the seed. Mace is a spice from the red membrane on the seed. People in faraway places paid a lot for both. Traders came from many places in Asia, and later from Europe. Banda's leaders were clever traders. They chose whom they sold to.
read.sections.0.simpler.note: "Bandanese" is not a name in Indonesian: "orang Banda" (the people of Banda) throughout, so the checker's "name not found" warning for "Bandanese" is expected.

read.sections.1.text.source: The Dutch East India Company, called the VOC, wanted a monopoly. It wanted to be the only buyer of Banda's nutmeg, so no one else could compete. In 1609, a VOC fleet came to Banda Neira, one of the islands, and began to build a fort. The people there refused the company's demands, and years of fighting followed. In 1621, a VOC force led by Jan Pieterszoon Coen attacked the islands. Many Bandanese people were killed. Others were enslaved or forced to leave. Some escaped to other islands, where people kept Banda's history alive in songs and dances. After 1621, the VOC gave the land to settlers, and enslaved people were forced to grow the nutmeg.
read.sections.1.text.back: The Dutch East India Company, called the VOC, wanted a monopoly. The VOC wanted to be the only buyer of nutmeg from Banda, so that no other party could compete. In 1609, a VOC fleet came to Banda Neira, one of the islands there, and began to build a fort. The people there refused the company's demands, and years of fighting followed. In 1621, a VOC force led by Jan Pieterszoon Coen attacked the islands. Many Bandanese people were killed. Others were enslaved or forced to leave. Some managed to escape to other islands, and there people kept Banda's history alive through songs and dances. After 1621, the VOC gave the land to settlers, and enslaved people were forced to grow nutmeg.
read.sections.1.text.note: The violence is stated plainly and once, as in the English: "dibunuh" (killed), "diperbudak" (enslaved), "dipaksa pergi" (forced to leave). Please check the tone with particular care.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: A Dutch company called the VOC came to Banda. It wanted a monopoly. It wanted to be the only buyer of nutmeg. In 1609, it began to build a fort. The people of Banda said no. They fought for years. In 1621, the VOC attacked again. Many Bandanese people were killed. Others were made slaves or forced to leave. Some escaped to other islands. They kept Banda's history alive in songs and dances. Then enslaved people had to grow the nutmeg.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: A Dutch company called the VOC came to Banda. The VOC wanted a monopoly. The VOC wanted to be the only buyer of nutmeg. In 1609, the VOC began to build a fort. The people of Banda refused. They fought for years. In 1621, the VOC attacked again. Many Bandanese people were killed. Others were made slaves or forced to leave. Some managed to escape to other islands. They kept Banda's history alive through songs and dances. Then enslaved people had to grow nutmeg.
read.sections.1.simpler.note: "Were made slaves" → "dijadikan budak", as the English simpler text says; "diperbudak" is used everywhere else.

read.sections.2.heading.back: A picture owned by the company, made later

read.sections.2.text.source: The second picture is a painting of Banda Neira from about 1662, more than 40 years after the attack. The VOC paid a painters' workshop in the Netherlands to make it. It shows forts, a ship, houses and neat rows of nutmeg trees. It does not show the people who were harmed, or the people who worked in those gardens. The painting shows the company's perspective. Coen's own reports from 1621 are company sources too. In his letters, he wrote that almost nobody escaped, but that was not true. So historians compare sources, and they also listen to the songs and stories that Bandanese people passed down.
read.sections.2.text.back: The second picture is a painting of Banda Neira from about 1662, more than 40 years after that attack. The VOC paid a painters' workshop in the Netherlands to make it. This painting shows forts, a ship, houses and neat rows of nutmeg trees. This painting does not show the people who were harmed, or the people who worked in those gardens. This painting shows the company's point of view. Coen's own reports from 1621 are also company sources. In his letters, he wrote that almost nobody escaped, but that was not true. So historians compare sources, and they also listen to the songs and stories passed down by Bandanese people.
read.sections.2.text.note: "The people who were harmed" → "orang-orang yang dicelakai". "Dirugikan" would be weaker (financially harmed); "disakiti" (hurt) is an alternative.

It does not show the people who were hurt. It shows the company's perspective. Coen wrote reports too. He said almost nobody escaped. That was not true. So historians check many sources. They also listen to Bandanese songs and stories.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: This lesson covers the VOC's conquest of Banda in 1621: mass killing, enslavement and forced removal. The Dutch National Archives' teaching page is titled “Genocide op Banda (1621)”. Learner text states it plainly, once, with no detail and no death toll; sources give different numbers (the archives: up to 15,000 people before, about 1,000 left on the islands; the Rijksmuseum: all 15,000 killed or driven away), so never ask learners to learn a figure. Some learners may have lived through violence or forced displacement: say before part 2 what it covers, let anyone read the simpler text or step away, and never ask learners about their own or their family's experiences of war, displacement, their country, religion or ethnicity. Don't present the events as a disagreement with two equal sides, and never invent a Bandanese first-person quotation. The TED-Ed video describes the violence in far more detail than the lesson (see its note): preview it first.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: This lesson covers the VOC's conquest of Banda in 1621: mass killing, enslavement and forced removal. The Dutch National Archives' learning page is titled “Genocide op Banda (1621)” (Genocide on Banda). The learners' text names it plainly, once, without detail and without a death toll; sources give different figures (the archives: up to 15,000 people before, about 1,000 left on the islands; the Rijksmuseum: all 15,000 people killed or driven out), so never ask learners to memorise a figure. Some learners may have experienced violence or forced removal: say before part 2 what it contains, let anyone read the simpler version or step away for a while, and never ask learners about their own or their family's experiences of war, displacement, their country, religion or ethnicity. Do not present these events as a dispute between two equal sides, and never make up a first-person quotation from a Bandanese person. The TED-Ed video describes the violence in far more detail than this lesson (see its note): watch it first.
sensitiveNotes.0.note: "Genocide" → "genosida", the standard Indonesian term, in the gloss of the archive's title only, as the English uses it only there. "Forced displacement" → "pengusiran paksa"; "displacement" (as refugees) → "pengungsian".

educatorNotes.0.source: Aim: learners name the VOC's monopoly and the harm it brought, and say whose account a company source leaves out. Evidence move (brief 3B): read Coen's report as a company source (he led the attack, and the archives show his claim that almost nobody escaped was false: about 1,700 Bandanese escaped), then look at the later commissioned painting. A sound answer names the monopoly and the harm and identifies a missing account. Misconception to catch: a fort or an orderly ship in the painting does not prove trade was voluntary or that the VOC caused no harm. Banda's history did not end in 1621: people who escaped kept it alive, for example in the Kei Islands, through songs and dances such as the Wanar dance (Dutch National Archives).
educatorNotes.0.back: Aim: learners name the VOC's monopoly and the harm it brought, and say whose story is missing from a source owned by the company. Step for reading the evidence (brief 3B): read Coen's report as a company source (he led that attack, and the archives show that his claim that almost nobody escaped was false: about 1,700 Bandanese people escaped), then look at the painting commissioned later. A good answer names the monopoly and its harm and recognises a missing story. Misunderstanding to watch for: an orderly fort or ship in the painting does not prove that the trade was voluntary or that the VOC caused no harm. Banda's history did not end in 1621: the people who escaped kept it alive, for example in the Kei Islands, through songs and dances such as the Wanar dance (Dutch National Archives).

educatorNotes.1.source: Source caveats: the Dutch National Archives says its collection holds no sources with Bandanese voices, so every archive source on Banda tells the story from a colonial view. Its page shows Coen's 6 May 1621 report on the decision to starve out Banda Besar; the lesson describes it only in general terms and never quotes it. The Rijksmuseum says the painting was commissioned by the VOC's Amsterdam chamber from the Vingboons workshop before 30 April 1663, probably for the directors' meeting room, and was based on company maps: Neira never had five nutmeg gardens, and the hills behind are imagined. Before the VOC, the Westfries Museum says Dutch traders at first paid port fees and bought spice like other visitors, which helps show the change from trade to force.
